title: Gradients
learningObjectives: Explain gradients and apply it correctly in a small CSS example.

understand.concept: CSS gradients are generated images that transition between colours. Common forms include linear-gradient(), radial-gradient(), and conic-gradient(). They can be used anywhere an image value is accepted, including background-image.
understand.whyItMatters: A gradient needs at least two colour stops. Linear gradients follow a direction or angle; radial gradients spread from a point or shape; conic gradients sweep around a centre. Multiple stops can control where transitions occur.
understand.analogy: A gradient resembles a smooth blend between paint samples, but the browser calculates the pixels rather than using a physical mixture.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy helps build intuition, but the browser follows the CSS specifications and computed-style rules rather than human intentions.

explain.narrative: The panel transitions from dark teal through green to warm yellow. Change the angle or stop positions.

examples.explanation: The panel transitions from dark teal through green to warm yellow. Change the angle or stop positions.

practise.guidedTask: Create one linear gradient with three stops and one radial gradient. Use each as a separate card background.
practise.independentTask: Which function creates a circular or elliptical colour transition from a centre?
